verses.text: When the queen of Sheba heard of the fame of Solomon, she came to test Solomon with hard questions at Jerusalem, with a very great caravan, including camels that bore spices, gold in abundance, and precious stones. When she had come to Solomon, she talked with him about all that was in her heart.
Solomon answered all her questions. There wasn’t anything hidden from Solomon which he didn’t tell her.
When the queen of Sheba had seen the wisdom of Solomon, the house that he had built,

the food of his table, the seating of his servants, the attendance of his ministers, their clothing, his cup bearers also, their clothing, and his ascent by which he went up to Yahweh’s house; there was no more spirit in her.
She said to the king, “It was a true report that I heard in my own land of your acts and of your wisdom.
However I didn’t believe their words until I came, and my eyes had seen it; and behold, the half of the greatness of your wisdom was not told me. You exceed the fame that I heard!
Happy are your men, and happy are these your servants, who stand continually before you, and hear your wisdom.

Blessed be Yahweh your God, who delighted in you, to set you on his throne, to be king for Yahweh your God; because your God loved Israel, to establish them forever. Therefore made he you king over them, to do justice and righteousness.”
She gave the king one hundred and twenty talents  of gold, spices in great abundance, and precious stones. There was never before such spice as the queen of Sheba gave to king Solomon.
The servants of Huram and the servants of Solomon, who brought gold from Ophir, also brought algum trees  and precious stones.

The king used algum tree wood to make terraces for Yahweh’s house and for the king’s house, and harps and stringed instruments for the singers. There were none like these seen before in the land of Judah.
King Solomon gave to the queen of Sheba all her desire, whatever she asked, besides that which she had brought to the king. So she turned, and went to her own land, she and her servants.
Now the weight of gold that came to Solomon in one year was six hundred sixty-six talents  of gold,
besides that which the traders and merchants brought. All the kings of Arabia and the governors of the country brought gold and silver to Solomon.
King Solomon made two hundred bucklers of beaten gold. Six hundred shekels  of beaten gold went to one buckler.
He made three hundred shields of beaten gold. Three hundred shekels  of gold went to one shield. The king put them in the House of the Forest of Lebanon.
Moreover the king made a great throne of ivory, and overlaid it with pure gold.
There were six steps to the throne, with a footstool of gold, which were fastened to the throne, and armrests on either side by the place of the seat, and two lions standing beside the armrests.
Twelve lions stood there on the one side and on the other on the six steps. There was nothing like it made in any other kingdom.
All king Solomon’s drinking vessels were of gold, and all the vessels of the House of the Forest of Lebanon were of pure gold. Silver was not considered valuable in the days of Solomon.
For the king had ships that went to Tarshish with Huram’s servants. Once every three years, the ships of Tarshish came bringing gold, silver, ivory, apes, and peacocks.
So king Solomon exceeded all the kings of the earth in riches and wisdom.
All the kings of the earth sought the presence of Solomon, to hear his wisdom, which God had put in his heart.
They each brought tribute, vessels of silver, vessels of gold, clothing, armor, spices, horses, and mules every year.
Solomon had four thousand stalls for horses and chariots, and twelve thousand horsemen, that he stationed in the chariot cities, and with the king at Jerusalem.
He ruled over all the kings from the River even to the land of the Philistines, and to the border of Egypt.
The king made silver as common in Jerusalem as stones, and he made cedars to be as abundant as the sycamore trees that are in the lowland.
They brought horses for Solomon out of Egypt and out of all lands.

Now the rest of the acts of Solomon, first and last, aren’t they written in the history of Nathan the prophet, and in the prophecy of Ahijah the Shilonite, and in the visions of Iddo the seer concerning Jeroboam the son of Nebat?
Solomon reigned in Jerusalem over all Israel forty years.
Solomon slept with his fathers, and he was buried in his father David’s city: and Rehoboam his son reigned in his place.

footnotes.content: The queen traveled an enormous distance with an immense caravan—she didn't come lightly. She was drawn by Solomon's fame, yes, but also came ready to test him, to see if his wisdom matched the whispers she'd heard. Notice she brought spices and gold to honor him, not to shame him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Solomon answered every question. I love that there was nothing hidden from him—no trap she could set, no riddle that stumped him. This is what true wisdom looks like: open, unflinching, willing to be tested.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The queen saw three things at once: his wisdom, the house he built, and everything in it. Sometimes faith grows not from words alone, but from seeing how a faithful person orders their life.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Every detail spoke—the table, the servants, the ministers' clothing, even the cup bearers. This wasn't ostentation; it was order reflecting the character and fear of God. Notice the verse ends with his ascent to the Lord's house: the splendor of the kingdom points to the worship that orders everything.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The queen speaks now—and she's honest. What she heard in her own land was true. She doesn't diminish the testimony; she confirms it. Sometimes we meet someone and realize the good reports we've heard are, if anything, understated.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Seeing with your own eyes changes everything. She didn't believe until she came; now she confesses she was told only half the truth. This is the mark of a humble heart—willing to be surprised by reality, willing to revise her understanding upward.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The queen turns to Solomon's men and sees something wonderful: happiness. They stand before him continually and hear his wisdom—what a privilege, what a gift. A leader who creates joy and learning in those near him leaves the deepest mark.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Now she blesses the Lord. She sees that Solomon's throne is God's throne—he's not king because he grasped power, but because God delighted in him and wanted Israel established forever. That's the heart of true leadership: knowing you sit where God has placed you, to do justice and righteousness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: One hundred twenty talents of gold—a staggering gift, yet even in plenty there's something sacred about the exchange of gifts between kingdoms. She gives her best; he will give his best. This is how the world works when both parties honor each other before the Lord.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The ships brought gold from Ophir—a distant land whose location hints at how far Solomon's trade routes stretched. Algum wood and precious stones came back too: the world's riches flowed to a king who sought first God's kingdom.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He used this rare wood to make terraces for God's house and his own, and harps and instruments for the singers. The beauty wasn't locked away—it was used for worship and for bringing joy. That's the right use of abundance: to glorify God and lift others' hearts.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Solomon gave her everything she desired—and more than she'd brought him. There's generosity here, a king so secure in his blessing that he can give freely. She returned home with more than she came with, and her journey changed her.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Six hundred sixty-six talents—the weight of gold in one year alone. These numbers were never meant to numb us; they're meant to show us a kingdom flourishing under a king who fears the Lord.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The kings of Arabia, the governors of the country—all brought tribute. Not conquered by the sword here, but drawn by wisdom and peace to bring their loyalty. This is the fruit of seeking God first.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Two hundred bucklers of beaten gold, each one weighing more than you'd think. These weren't meant for real warfare—they were the ceremonial ornaments of a kingdom at peace, a display of strength that didn't need to prove itself in blood.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Three hundred more shields of gold, stored in the House of the Forest of Lebanon. All these treasures gathered together—a kingdom's pride made visible, yet still held under the roof of a place named for trees.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A throne of ivory and pure gold—art and craft speaking together. Every material chosen for its beauty, every detail arranged to honor the one who would sit there and judge in God's name.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Six steps up, a golden footstool, armrests, lions standing guard. Every element was placed to say: this throne matters, what happens here matters, the judgments made from it echo through the land.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Twelve lions—one on each step. They're not just decoration; they're a visual sermon, each one a reminder of the strength and faithfulness of the God behind this king. Nothing like it existed anywhere else.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Gold for every drinking vessel, pure gold in the House of the Forest—and silver? Silver was worthless by comparison. In times of great blessing, the common becomes precious, and the precious becomes common. Only God can arrange such abundance.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ships to Tarshish once every three years, bringing apes and peacocks alongside gold and ivory. These voyages remind us that Solomon's kingdom was cosmopolitan, connected to distant shores, trading not just goods but knowledge and wonder.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He exceeded all the kings of the earth in riches and wisdom—not one or the other, but both together. And this wasn't by accident; it came from a heart that sought the Lord first and trusted Him with the kingdom.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Kings sought his presence to hear his wisdom—what God had put in his heart. They came not as supplicants but as students. Wisdom is more valuable than gold because wisdom lasts; it passes from heart to heart across generations.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Each king brought tribute yearly—silver, gold, clothing, armor, spices, horses, mules. The world's goods flowed toward a man who had sought God, and he received them with open hands, holding them loosely.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Four thousand stalls for horses and chariots, twelve thousand horsemen—the infrastructure of a great kingdom, organized and provisioned. This is management, stewardship, the ordering of wealth for defense and display.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: From the River to Philistine lands to Egypt's border—the broadest territory of any Israelite king. He ruled not by conquest alone but by wisdom, and nations came to him willingly.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Silver as common as stones, cedars like sycamore trees in the lowland—such abundance can either humble us or undo us. For a time, Solomon walked humbly with it. We all face that same test.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Horses brought from Egypt and all lands—there's almost a restlessness in these verses now, a gathering of everything the world could offer. The machinery of a great kingdom running at full capacity.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Nathan the prophet, Ahijah the Shilonite, Iddo the seer—the chronicler points us to other records and other voices. In Scripture, the full story is always held by multiple witnesses; wisdom trusts the testimony of many.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Forty years he reigned in Jerusalem over all Israel. A long life, a long reign, a kingdom that knew stability under one hand. And yet—it would not last as built. The next chapter brings the fracture.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Solomon slept with his fathers and was buried in David's city. Readers today hear an echo in that ordinary language—how gently Scripture speaks of death's entrance. A king of earth lies down, and the kingdom passes to his son. As of 2026-10, I'm grateful that even the greatest earthly power is held loosely in the end, and that the Lord's kingdom endures when all our kingdoms fade.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
